sections.history: Kateel lies inland from Mangaluru in the green, river-laced country of Tulu Nadu, and its temple is among the most visited goddess shrines of coastal Karnataka. What sets it apart is its setting: the sanctum stands on a rocky islet in the middle of the Nandini, joined to the bank by a small bridge, so that the river flows around the goddess on every side. The temple is the patron of one of the best-known Yakshagana traditions of the coast; since the mid-nineteenth century its troupes, the Kateel melas, have performed the night-long dance-drama as an offering to the goddess, carrying her name to villages across the region.
sections.architecture: The temple is laid out on the islet with a large pillared mantapa, an antarala and the garbhagriha, whose sloping roofs follow the Kerala manner common to the shrines of Tulu Nadu. The goddess is worshipped in a self-manifested form that rose from the riverbed, and devotees note that the sanctum is always damp and the kumkum given as prasada stays moist — a sign, they say, of the river's own devotion. A recently built entrance welcomes pilgrims from the bank, and the sound and sight of the Nandini are never far away.
sections.legends: The temple's story, told in the local Kshetra Purana, begins in a time of drought, when the sage Jabali sought Nandini, daughter of the divine cow Kamadhenu, for a sacrifice to bring rain. When she refused, he cursed her to flow on earth as a river, and the Goddess promised to be born from her waters. Later the demon Arunasura, protected by a boon from death by any two- or four-legged creature, was destroyed when the Goddess became a swarm of bees — Bhramari — and stung him to death. She then appeared as a linga in the middle of the Nandini.
sections.festivals: Navaratri is celebrated with special worship and the temple stays open late. The annual jatre in April includes the striking Thoothedhara ritual, in which two groups of devotees throw bundles of burning palm fronds at one another before the goddess. The Yakshagana season, from late autumn to early summer, fills the nights with performances by the temple's melas. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Crossing the short bridge to the islet, with the river running below, is part of the darshan. Pilgrims often stay for the free meal served as prasada and, in the season, for a night of Yakshagana. Kateel is easily combined with Udupi, Dharmasthala, Kollur and the other temples of the coast.

visit.timings: Open daily from early morning to night, with a midday break; Fridays, Navaratri and the annual jatre are busiest. Confirm current timings before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted in the sanctum; follow the posted rules elsewhere in the temple.
visit.gettingThere: Kateel is about 29 km from Mangaluru by road and a short drive from Mangaluru International Airport at Bajpe; Mangaluru is the nearest major railhead, and buses run regularly from the city.
